name: Iris Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: These days I'm a lead finish carpenter on refurbishment jobs, mostly old schools and a hospital wing at the moment. My team of five does the second fix: doors, skirting, built-in cupboards, the handrails on the stairs, all the bits people actually touch. I love hanging a heavy fire door so it swings shut with that soft click. What wears me out is working round live buildings, nurses pushing trolleys past while you're trying to scribe a skirting board to a wonky wall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Old buildings with wonky walls sounds like its own skill. How did you end up doing that kind of work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started in new-build housing in my twenties, and I was the only woman on most sites, so I had to be twice as tidy to get half the credit. Then I found refurbishment suited me, because nothing is square and you have to think. I've got a little notebook for every job, and lately I'll sometimes ask one of those AI chat programs to tidy my snag list into something the client can read. My partner Tom laughs at me for being polite to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's what I expected, a handy helper for paperwork and not much more. Nobody's going to scribe a skirting board to a three-hundred-year-old wall with a chatbot. I might post that in the women-in-trades group I'm in, because there's been a lot of worry there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan holds. Five more years on the mortgage, work till about sixty-four or sixty-five, then cut down to part-time. Honestly it'd be a bit of a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. I'd keep using the chat program for snag lists and quotes, because it saves me maybe an hour on a Friday. And I'd keep pushing the firm to take on more women apprentices, which is my little crusade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Like the next five years are already drawn on the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your little crusade. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now it's Priya, nineteen, on her second year. I make sure she's not just sweeping up, she's hanging doors with me. Last month she fitted a whole run of cupboards on her own and I made the site manager come and look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd still be uneasy about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the bosses might use it as an excuse to squeeze the quotes tighter. If a program says a door takes forty minutes, someone's got to explain that a hospital door with a vision panel and closers takes two hours. That someone is usually me.

S0.say: It's what I expected: a handy helper for paperwork, not much more. Nobody scribes a skirting board to a three-hundred-year-old wall with a chatbot.
S0.think: Her plan holds: five more years on the mortgage, work until about sixty-four or sixty-five, then part-time. It would be a relief.
S0.do: Keeps working as she is and uses the chat program to save about an hour a week on snag lists and quotes. Keeps pushing her firm to take on more women apprentices.
S0.feel: Calm, as if the next five years are already drawn on the plan.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to scribe a skirting board to a three-hundred-year-old wall with a chatbot.
S0.fieldNote: She already uses AI occasionally, for paperwork only, and is relaxed about it. Her energy goes into mentoring young women in the trade, especially her apprentice Priya. The only edge of worry is that software might be used to squeeze job times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine as long as workers get a say in it. If a firm brings in machines, the people doing the job should help decide how, and get trained on paid time. I'd say that at my union branch and probably to the site manager over a brew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think refurbishment is about the last place it bites, because every old building is different. New-build is where I'd expect the factory-made panels and the robots. So for me it's mostly fine, but Tom worries me more than I do, because he drives a bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short course on whatever new digital tools come in, the scanning kit that measures a room, that kind of thing, once I'd seen it work on another site. I'd sit down with Tom and look at whether we can pay off the mortgage a bit faster, maybe an extra hundred a month. And I'd make sure Priya gets on any training going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly on Tom's behalf. For myself I feel I'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Tom's job worry you more than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because driving is exactly the kind of thing they've been promising to automate for years. He's fifty-nine, he's done the number nine route for sixteen years, and he loves it. If they cut drivers, he's not going to become a computer programmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until you'd seen the new kit work on another site. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen plenty of gadgets turn up with a big launch and end up in the back of the van. Remember the laser measure that got everything wrong near glass? Once a couple of sites I trust are using something and swearing by it, I'll learn it properly.

S1.say: Change is fine as long as workers get a say. People doing the job should help decide how machines come in, with training on paid time.
S1.think: Refurbishment is about the last place it bites, because every old building is different. She's more worried about her partner Tom, who drives a bus.
S1.do: Takes a short course on proven digital tools like room-scanning kit once she has seen them work elsewhere. Adds about a hundred a month to mortgage payments and gets her apprentice onto any training going.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for Tom; for herself she feels she'd manage.
S1.quote: I've seen plenty of gadgets turn up with a big launch and end up in the back of the van.
S1.fieldNote: She sees her own corner of the trade as well protected, so her worry moves to her partner's bus job. Her approach to new tools is to wait for proof from trusted sites, then learn properly. Her politics come through as wanting workers to have a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when we let tech firms run ahead of the law. There should have been rules and a safety net before it was switched on. I'd be saying it loudly at the union and I'd write to our local representative, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a double hit. Tom's bus goes driverless, probably first, and then my work dries up a year or two later, and we've still got five years on the mortgage. With about three months of savings, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, we'd stop the extra on the mortgage and build the savings instead, every spare bit, and drop the new kitchen we've been planning. I'd get onto the union about redundancy terms for older staff. I'd also ask the bank about stretching the mortgage before we're in trouble, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. Like getting the call that the scaffold's come down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd write to your representative. What would the letter actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a fifty-eight-year-old who's hung fire doors in their hospitals for thirty years shouldn't lose her house because a company in another country built a better robot. Then I'd ask them what the plan is, in writing. I'd want a date and a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya, your apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest bit. I'd want to tell her to stay, because she's so good, but I couldn't in good conscience. I think I'd tell her to finish her ticket anyway, so she has it, and keep her options open, and I'd hate myself a bit for saying it.

S2.say: This is what happens when tech firms run ahead of the law. There should have been rules and a safety net before it was switched on.
S2.think: It would be a double hit: Tom's bus job first, hers a year or two later, with five years left on the mortgage. With about three months of savings, that frightens her.
S2.do: Stops overpaying the mortgage, drops the planned kitchen and builds savings with every spare bit. Presses the union on redundancy terms for older staff, writes to her local representative, and asks the bank early about stretching the mortgage.
S2.feel: Sick to her stomach, like hearing that the scaffold has come down.
S2.quote: A fifty-eight-year-old who's hung fire doors in their hospitals for thirty years shouldn't lose her house because a company in another country built a better robot.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline turns her from calm to alarmed, largely because both household incomes are exposed at once and the mortgage still has five years to run. She'd act early and practically, talking to the bank before trouble. Advising her apprentice to keep her options open clearly pains her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so the government has no excuse not to. Retraining money, a pension bridge, rules on how fast firms can lay people off. I'd say it like I'm reading a shopping list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three and the mortgage is nearly done, maybe a year left. That's a totally different story to the two-year one. It's tight, but I think we'd scrape through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare penny on the mortgage, maybe two hundred extra a month, to clear it before 2031. I'd look at moving into a site inspection or clerk of works job, checking other people's work, which is something I'd fancy anyway and a machine might take longer to be trusted with. Tom would look at what his firm offers older drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but in a way I can work with. Like a tight deadline on a job I know I can hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The clerk of works idea is new. What makes you think a machine would take longer to be trusted with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when a building goes wrong, someone has to sign their name and stand in front of a judge. I can't see clients trusting a robot's signature on fire doors in a hospital, not for a while. I don't really know, mind, it's a hunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in the faster picture you'd be sick to your stomach. What makes three extra years so different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage. It's that simple. In two years we owe a lot, in five we owe almost nothing, and once the roof's ours I can cope with nearly anything.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan properly, so the government has no excuse. It should provide retraining money, a pension bridge and rules on how fast firms can lay people off.
S3.think: By 2031 she's sixty-three with about a year left on the mortgage, which changes everything. It's tight, but she thinks they'd scrape through.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by about two hundred a month to clear it before 2031. Looks into moving to a site inspection or clerk of works role while Tom checks what his firm offers older drivers.
S3.feel: Tense, but in a workable way, like a tight deadline she knows she can hit.
S3.quote: In two years we owe a lot, in five we owe almost nothing, and once the roof's ours I can cope with nearly anything.
S3.fieldNote: For her the difference between the two AGI timelines comes down almost entirely to the mortgage balance. She produces a concrete fallback, inspection work, built on the idea that people will want a human signature. She's honest that it's only a hunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's use it to do it fairly. Shorter hours, retraining, decent pensions, the lot. If we can't sort it with ten years' notice, shame on all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'll be sixty-eight, mortgage paid, retired or doing a bit of part-time. It's the young ones like Priya and our two lads I'd think about. I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the plan: clear the mortgage, work till about sixty-four, then go part-time. I'd use the chat program a bit more to see how good it's getting, just to keep an eye on it. And I'd spend my last years making Priya the best finish carpenter in the county, while also telling her to learn the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about myself, with a bit of sadness about the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your two sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik's a paramedic, so I'd say his kind of job, with people in a crisis, probably lasts a while yet. Jonas works in an insurance office and that's the one I'd worry about. I'd tell him to start looking around now and not wait until he's my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sadness about the trade. What exactly would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The handing on. An old joiner taught me to hang a door, I taught Priya, and she'd have taught someone. If that stops with her, there's something lost that you can't print off.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so use it to do it fairly: shorter hours, retraining and decent pensions. If it can't be sorted with ten years' notice, shame on all of us.
S4.think: She'll be sixty-eight, mortgage paid and retired or part-time, so she'd be all right. Her concern is for her apprentice Priya and her two sons.
S4.do: Sticks to the plan of clearing the mortgage and working until about sixty-four before going part-time. Uses the chat program a little more to track how good it's getting, and trains Priya hard while urging her to learn the machines.
S4.feel: Calm about herself, with some sadness about the trade.
S4.quote: An old joiner taught me to hang a door, I taught Priya, and she'd have taught someone.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade her personal risk fades, and her feeling becomes grief for the chain of skill passed hand to hand. She worries most about her son in an insurance office. She stays measured and practical, keeping an eye on the tools rather than ignoring them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits Tom and me both while we've still got the mortgage. What would help is a bit of breathing space: a mortgage holiday scheme, and a payment to tide older workers over to pension. And a real say for unions in how it's all brought in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in the trade. It took us forty years to get a few of us onto sites, and I'd hate it if the robots came just as we'd got through the gate.

headlineQuote: It took us forty years to get a few of us onto sites, and I'd hate it if the robots came just as we'd got through the gate.
portrait: Iris is a fifty-eight-year-old lead finish carpenter on school and hospital refurbishments, one of few women of her generation in the trade, who mentors a young apprentice named Priya. She uses an AI chat program now and then for paperwork and adopts new tools once she's seen them proven. With five years left on the mortgage and a partner who drives a bus, the two-year AGI picture alarms her as a double hit on the household. With five or ten years, the paid-off mortgage makes her steady, and she eyes inspection work. Her politics show in a steady call for rules, safety nets and a say for workers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit both her and her bus-driver partner while they still have five years on the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A mortgage holiday scheme, a payment to tide older workers over to pension, and a real say for unions in how the change is brought in.
